# SQL

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(dslabs)
```

## 1. Loading the datasets

We load the dengue and influenza datasets from local CSV files.
The Gapminder dataset is loaded from the dslabs package.

```{r}
dengue <- read_csv("data/dengue_data.csv", skip = 11)

flu <- read_csv("data/flu_data.csv", skip = 11)

gapminder_data <- dslabs::gapminder
```

## 2. Checking and tidying the datasets

The dengue and flu datasets are initially stored in wide format, 
with each country represented by a separate column. We transform 
these datasets into long format using `pivot_longer()`.

```{r}
dengue_tidy <- dengue %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Date,
    names_to = "country",
    values_to = "dengue"
  )

flu_tidy <- flu %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Date,
    names_to = "country",
    values_to = "flu"
  )
```

## 3. Standardizing country and date variables

The dengue and flu datasets contain a weekly `Date` variable, while Gapminder contains a yearly `year` variable. Additionally, `country` is stored as a factor in Gapminder and as a character in the other datasets.

To make the datasets compatible for joining, we standardize these variables.

```{r}
dengue_tidy <- dengue_tidy %>%
  mutate(
    country = as.character(country),
    year = as.integer(substr(Date, 1, 4))
  )

flu_tidy <- flu_tidy %>%
  mutate(
    country = as.character(country),
    year = as.integer(substr(Date, 1, 4))
  )

gapminder_tidy <- gapminder_data %>%
  mutate(country = as.character(country))

# Check data types
class(dengue_tidy$country)
class(flu_tidy$country)
class(gapminder_tidy$country)

class(dengue_tidy$year)
class(flu_tidy$year)
class(gapminder_tidy$year)
```

The datasets now have matching data types for `country` (character) and `year` (integer). The original weekly `Date` variable is retained in the dengue and flu datasets.

## 4. Checking country names

We check the country names in each dataset to see which countries are included.

```{r}
sort(unique(dengue_tidy$country))
sort(unique(flu_tidy$country))
sort(unique(gapminder_tidy$country))
```

The country names are consistent across the three datasets. However, the datasets contain different numbers of countries. Therefore, we will use only countries that are present in all three datasets.

## 5. Preparing the datasets for joining

Only countries present in all three datasets are selected. The weekly dengue and flu data are then summarized into yearly averages to match the yearly Gapminder data.

```{r}
# Select countries present in all three datasets
common_countries <- unique(dengue_tidy$country[
  dengue_tidy$country %in% flu_tidy$country &
  dengue_tidy$country %in% gapminder_tidy$country])

# Filter all datasets
dengue_tidy <- dengue_tidy %>%
  filter(country %in% common_countries)

flu_tidy <- flu_tidy %>%
  filter(country %in% common_countries)

gapminder_tidy <- gapminder_tidy %>%
  filter(country %in% common_countries)

# Calculate yearly averages
dengue_yearly <- dengue_tidy %>%
  group_by(country, year) %>%
  summarise(dengue = mean(dengue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

flu_yearly <- flu_tidy %>%
  group_by(country, year) %>%
  summarise(flu = mean(flu, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

## 6. Saving the datasets

The three prepared datasets are saved as CSV files so they can be imported into PostgreSQL.

```{r}
write_csv(dengue_yearly, "data/dengue_yearly.csv")
write_csv(flu_yearly, "data/flu_yearly.csv")
write_csv(gapminder_tidy, "data/gapminder.csv")
```
